valid_transformations.notes: O₂ is paramagnetic (2 unpaired). N₂ is diamagnetic. Co²⁺ (d⁷) with high spin has 3 unpaired? Actually d⁷: t₂g⁵ eg² → 3 unpaired (if high spin) → paramagnetic.

valid_transformations.to: Identify element and its properties (Z, block, period, group)
reagents: Sum electrons = Z; last electron determines block (s,p,d,f) and period.
valid_transformations.mechanism: Sum Z; block = last orbital (s,p,d,f); period = highest n; group = valence electrons count (for s,p).

expand_comparison_set.description: Additional modifications for d-block trends; kept minimal.

conceptual_fragility.description: All fragile concepts and common mistakes from Chapter 3.

concepts.name: VSEPR confusion: electron-pair geometry vs molecular shape
concepts.explanation: Electron-pair geometry includes lone pairs; molecular shape ignores them.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often give electron-pair geometry when molecular shape is asked.

concepts.name: Hybridization and geometry: sp³ can be tetrahedral, pyramidal, or bent
concepts.explanation: The hybridization only describes the mixing of orbitals, not the shape.
concepts.why_fragile: Assuming sp³ always tetrahedral.

concepts.name: Back bonding: when and how it affects properties
concepts.explanation: Requires vacant d or p orbital on acceptor; shortens bond length and alters angles.
concepts.why_fragile: Students forget to consider back bonding in angle comparisons.
concepts.common_error: Predicting PF₃ angle < PH₃ based on electronegativity (it's actually >).

concepts.name: Drago's rule: lack of hybridization in heavier hydrides
concepts.explanation: For PH₃, AsH₃, etc., the lone pair is in an s orbital, bonding in p orbitals, angles ~90°.
concepts.why_fragile: Students apply sp³ to all AH₃.

concepts.name: MO theory: s–p mixing and order of MOs
concepts.explanation: For B₂, C₂, N₂, π2p is lower than σ2p due to mixing; for O₂, F₂, σ2p is lower.
concepts.why_fragile: Using same order for all diatomics.
concepts.common_error: Predicting O₂ with N₂ order; wrong paramagnetism.

concepts.name: Radius ratio: predicting structures
concepts.explanation: Radius ratio gives coordination number but not always exact structure.
concepts.why_fragile: Over-reliance on radius ratio; other factors (polarization) matter.

concepts.name: Lattice energy and solubility: not directly correlated
concepts.explanation: Solubility depends on hydration energy and entropy as well.
concepts.why_fragile: Assuming higher lattice energy → less soluble (sometimes hydration dominates).
concepts.common_error: Predicting LiF soluble because Li⁺ small (it's sparingly soluble).

concepts.name: Fajans' rules: covalent character increases with polarizing power
concepts.explanation: Small cations, large anions, high charges, non-noble gas configurations increase covalency.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not consider non-noble gas configuration (e.g., Ag⁺).
concepts.common_error: Assuming NaCl and AgCl have similar ionic character.

concepts.name: Defects: distinguishing Schottky and Frenkel
concepts.explanation: Schottky: cation and anion vacancies; Frenkel: cation interstitial + vacancy.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing which occurs in which compound.

concepts.name: Band theory: conductors, semiconductors, insulators
concepts.explanation: Band gap determines classification; doping creates n- or p-type.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.
concepts.common_error: Thinking pure Si is a conductor (it's a semiconductor).

concepts.name: Dipole moment: lone pair contribution
concepts.explanation: Lone pairs contribute to dipole moment if in hybrid orbitals.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often ignore lone pair moments.
concepts.common_error: Predicting NF₃ μ=0 (it's not; it has small but non-zero μ).

concepts.name: Resonance: bond order and bond length
concepts.explanation: Resonance averages bond orders; shorter bonds than single.
concepts.why_fragile: Forgetting resonance in bond length comparisons.
concepts.common_error: Assuming all N–O bonds in NO₃⁻ are single bonds.

concepts.name: Born–Haber cycle: sign conventions
concepts.explanation: Lattice energy is negative (exothermic), EA negative.
concepts.why_fragile: Mixing signs in calculations.
concepts.common_error: Using positive lattice energy in cycle.

concepts.name: F-centres: colour and paramagnetism
concepts.explanation: Unpaired electrons in anion vacancies cause colour and paramagnetism.
concepts.why_fragile: Not connecting F-centres with colour.
concepts.common_error: Thinking colour in NaCl is due to impurities.

concepts.standard_case: All polydentate ligands are chelating.
concepts.exception: NH₂–NH₂ (hydrazine) and N(CH₂CH₂)₃N (triethylenediamine) cannot act as chelating ligands because hydrazine would form a strained 3‑membered ring and triethylenediamine has a locked bridgehead structure.
concepts.trap: Assuming any ligand with multiple donor atoms chelates.
concepts.why_exception: Ring strain or rigid geometry prevents chelation.

concepts.standard_case: Ligands donate 2 electrons (one lone pair).
concepts.exception: NO can act as a 3‑electron donor (lone pair + one electron from π* orbital) in complexes like [Fe(CO)₂(NO)₂].
concepts.trap: Always treating NO as a 2‑electron donor.
concepts.why_exception: The antibonding electron of NO is easily donated.

concepts.standard_case: Sidgwick EAN rule: complex is stable if EAN equals the next noble gas configuration.
concepts.exception: Many stable complexes do not obey the EAN rule, e.g., [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ (EAN=35), [PtCl₄]²⁻ (EAN=84), [PdCl₄]²⁻ (EAN=52), [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ (EAN=35).
concepts.why_exception: The rule works best for low‑oxidation‑state carbonyls; it fails for many coordination compounds.

concepts.standard_case: Square planar geometry occurs only for d⁸ metal ions with strong field ligands.
concepts.exception: Square planar also occurs for d⁴ (Cr(II) with weak ligands), d⁶ (Fe(II) in haem), d⁷ (Co(II) with strong ligands), and d⁹ (Cu²⁺, Ag²⁺ with both strong and weak ligands).
concepts.trap: Thinking only d⁸ gives square planar.
concepts.why_exception: Electronic configurations and ligand field strength can stabilise square planar for other d counts.

concepts.standard_case: Tetrahedral complexes can be low spin if ligands are strong enough.
concepts.exception: All tetrahedral complexes are high spin because Δₜ ≈ 4/9 Δ₀ and is always smaller than pairing energy P.
concepts.trap: Assuming strong field ligands cause low spin even in tetrahedral geometry.
concepts.why_exception: Tetrahedral splitting is too small to overcome pairing energy.

concepts.standard_case: SnCl₂ can act as a ligand (Lewis base).
concepts.exception: SnCl₂ does not act as a ligand, but SnCl₃⁻ does. The lone pair in SnCl₂ has high s‑character (less available), while in SnCl₃⁻ the lone pair acquires more p‑character (better donor).
concepts.trap: Assuming all tin chlorides are good ligands.
concepts.why_exception: s‑character effect on lone pair availability.
concepts.exam_relevance: Ligand properties of SnCl₂ vs SnCl₃⁻.

concepts.standard_case: Higher charge on metal ion means stronger acid (hydrolysis).
concepts.exception: [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is more acidic than [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ despite both being +3; Cr³⁺ is smaller and has higher charge density, so it polarises water more strongly.
concepts.trap: Comparing only oxidation state without size.
concepts.why_exception: Charge density (charge/radius) matters.

concepts.standard_case: Colour in transition metal complexes arises only from d‑d transitions.
concepts.exception: Complexes with d⁰ (MnO₄⁻, CrO₄²⁻) and d¹⁰ (CdS) are coloured due to charge‑transfer transitions, not d‑d.
concepts.trap: Assuming colour always requires unpaired d electrons.
concepts.why_exception: Ligand‑to‑metal charge transfer (LMCT) or metal‑to‑ligand charge transfer (MLCT) can give intense colours.

concepts.standard_case: Flexidentate ligands have fixed denticity.
concepts.exception: Some ligands (e.g., SCN⁻) can change denticity (monodentate or bridging) depending on conditions – called flexidentate.
concepts.why_exception: Ligand can use different numbers of donor atoms.

concepts.standard_case: Ligands are usually neutral or anionic.
concepts.exception: Cationic ligands exist, e.g., NO⁺ (nitrosylium) and hydrazinium (NH₂NH₃⁺).
concepts.trap: Only considering neutral or anionic ligands.
concepts.why_exception: Some positively charged species can donate electrons.

concepts.standard_case: EDTA⁴⁻ is always hexadentate.
concepts.exception: EDTA³⁻ (partially deprotonated) is pentadentate (one carboxylate group not coordinated).
concepts.why_exception: Protonation state affects denticity.

concepts.standard_case: [M(AA)₂] square planar complexes have no geometrical isomerism.
concepts.exception: If the bidentate ligand AA is chiral (e.g., bn = butylenediamine), geometrical (cis/trans) isomers exist.
concepts.why_exception: Chiral ligand creates distinct arrangements.

concepts.standard_case: Binuclear square planar complexes do not show geometrical isomerism.
concepts.exception: [Pd₂Cl₄(PPh₃)₂] shows geometrical isomerism (cis/trans around the Pd–Pd or bridging chloride arrangement).
concepts.trap: Assuming binuclear complexes are always simple.
concepts.why_exception: Different ligand arrangements around two metal centres.

concepts.standard_case: All five‑coordinate complexes are trigonal bipyramidal.
concepts.exception: Five‑coordinate complexes can also be square pyramidal (allogon isomers).
concepts.why_exception: Both geometries are possible for coordination number 5.

concepts.standard_case: Octahedral [M(AB)₃] (AB = unsymmetrical bidentate) has only two geometrical isomers (fac/mer).
concepts.exception: Each geometrical isomer (fac and mer) has an enantiomeric pair, giving a total of 4 stereoisomers (2 geometrical × 2 optical).
concepts.why_exception: Unsymmetrical bidentate creates chirality.

concepts.standard_case: Octahedral [M(AA)abcd] has 3 or 4 geometrical isomers.
concepts.exception: It has 6 geometrical isomers (according to the table in the chapter).
concepts.why_exception: More arrangements due to four different monodentate ligands.

concepts.standard_case: Octahedral [M(AB)abcd] (AB = unsymmetrical bidentate) has 6 geometrical isomers.
concepts.exception: It has 12 geometrical isomers (maximum for octahedral).
concepts.trap: Underestimating due to additional orientation of AB.
concepts.why_exception: Unsymmetrical bidentate adds extra arrangements.

concepts.standard_case: Square planar [Mabcd] has only 2 geometrical isomers.
concepts.exception: It has 3 geometrical isomers (different arrangements of four different ligands).
concepts.why_exception: With four different ligands, multiple arrangements are possible.

concepts.standard_case: Square planar [M(AB)₂] (AB = unsymmetrical bidentate) has no geometrical isomerism.
concepts.exception: It has 2 geometrical isomers (cis and trans).
concepts.trap: Assuming unsymmetrical bidentate always gives no isomers.
concepts.why_exception: Different orientations of AB create distinct arrangements.

concepts.standard_case: Square planar [M(AB)ab] has only one geometrical isomer.
concepts.exception: It has 2 geometrical isomers.
concepts.why_exception: Different positions of a and b relative to AB.

concepts.standard_case: Hydrate isomerism of CrCl₃·6H₂O gives only two isomers.
concepts.exception: It gives four isomers: [Cr(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ (violet), [Cr(H₂O)₅Cl]Cl₂·H₂O (bright green), [Cr(H₂O)₄Cl₂]Cl·2H₂O (dark green), and [Cr(H₂O)₃Cl₃]·3H₂O (dark green).
concepts.why_exception: Different numbers of water molecules in the coordination sphere.

concepts.standard_case: Ionization isomerism only involves exchange of anions between coordination sphere and outside.
concepts.exception: It can also occur with neutral ligands (e.g., solvent isomerism) when a solvent molecule is exchanged.
concepts.why_exception: Any ligand (neutral or charged) can be exchanged.

concepts.standard_case: Linkage isomerism only for NO₂⁻.
concepts.exception: Many ligands show linkage isomerism: SCN⁻ (thiocyanato vs isothiocyanato), CN⁻ (cyanido vs isocyanido), OCN⁻ (cyanato vs isocyanato), S₂O₃²⁻, etc.
concepts.why_exception: Any ambidentate ligand can show linkage isomerism.

concepts.standard_case: In linkage isomerism, M–SCN is linear like M–NCS.
concepts.exception: In Pd complexes, Pd–NCS is linear, but Pd–SCN is bent (∠Pd–S–C ≈ 107°).
concepts.why_exception: Different bonding modes affect geometry.

concepts.standard_case: Synergic bonding only strengthens the metal–ligand bond; it does not affect the ligand.
concepts.exception: Synergic bonding weakens the ligand internal bond (e.g., C–O bond order decreases in metal carbonyls).
concepts.trap: Thinking back‑donation only affects M–L bond.
concepts.why_exception: Electrons fill ligand π* orbitals, weakening ligand bond.
concepts.exam_relevance: Spectrochemical series and CO stretching frequencies.

concepts.standard_case: CFSE is always negative (stabilising).
concepts.exception: CFSE is zero for d⁰, d⁵ (high spin), and d¹⁰ configurations.
concepts.trap: Assuming all configurations have some stabilisation.
concepts.why_exception: Symmetrical filling gives no net stabilisation.

concepts.standard_case: Ionic radii of M²⁺ ions decrease smoothly across the first transition series.
concepts.exception: The decrease is not monotonic; Mn²⁺ has a larger radius than expected due to e₉ shielding, and the curve shows a double‑humped pattern.
concepts.why_exception: CFSE and d‑electron shielding affect radii.

concepts.standard_case: Hydration energies of M²⁺ ions decrease smoothly.
concepts.exception: Hydration energies show a double‑humped curve, with minima at d⁰, d⁵, and d¹⁰ (zero CFSE).
concepts.why_exception: CFSE contributes extra stabilisation.

concepts.standard_case: Jahn‑Teller distortion occurs for any asymmetrically filled d orbital set.
concepts.exception: Only distortions from e₉ configurations (d⁴ high spin, d⁷ low spin, d⁹) are significant; t₂g distortions are too small to detect.
concepts.trap: Applying Jahn‑Teller to all asymmetrical cases.
concepts.why_exception: e₉ orbitals point directly at ligands, so distortion is large.

concepts.standard_case: NH₃ and pyridine have very different Δ₀ values.
concepts.exception: In the spectrochemical series, NH₃ and pyridine have nearly equal Δ₀ (they are placed together).
concepts.why_exception: Similar ligand field strength.

concepts.standard_case: All Co³⁺ complexes are low spin (diamagnetic).
concepts.exception: [CoF₆]³⁻ is high spin (paramagnetic) because F⁻ is a weak field ligand (Δ₀ < P).
concepts.why_exception: Weak field ligands give high spin.

concepts.standard_case: All inner orbital complexes are low spin and all outer orbital complexes are high spin.
concepts.exception: This is generally true, but some inner orbital complexes may still have unpaired electrons (e.g., [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is inner orbital but has one unpaired electron, so it is low spin but not diamagnetic).
concepts.why_exception: Inner orbital means (n-1)d orbitals used, but if not all electrons are paired, it can still be paramagnetic.

concepts.standard_case: All square planar complexes are diamagnetic.
concepts.exception: Square planar complexes of d⁷ (e.g., Co(II) with strong field) have one unpaired electron (paramagnetic), and d⁹ (Cu²⁺) have one unpaired electron.
concepts.why_exception: d⁷ and d⁹ configurations leave unpaired electrons.

concepts.standard_case: Tetrahedral complexes are always paramagnetic (have unpaired electrons).
concepts.exception: Tetrahedral complexes with d⁰, d⁵ (high spin), and d¹⁰ have zero unpaired electrons (diamagnetic) because their configurations are symmetric (e.g., [ZnCl₄]²⁻ is diamagnetic).
concepts.why_exception: d⁰, d⁵, d¹⁰ give no unpaired electrons.

concepts.standard_case: The spectrochemical series is fixed and independent of metal.
concepts.exception: The order of ligands is practically constant for most metals, but the exact position can vary slightly depending on the metal and its oxidation state (though generally the series holds).
concepts.why_exception: Metal–ligand interactions can slightly alter the order.

concepts.name: Transition elements: definition
concepts.explanation: Transition elements are those with incompletely filled d orbitals in their ground state or in common oxidation states. Zn, Cd, Hg are d-block but not transition elements.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often call all d-block elements transition elements.

concepts.name: Variable oxidation states and stability
concepts.explanation: Stability of oxidation states depends on the metal and ligand; higher oxidation states are stabilised by oxygen/fluorine, lower by heavier halides.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may assume all oxidation states are equally stable.
concepts.common_error: Assuming Fe(VI) is as stable as Fe(III).

concepts.name: Colour due to d-d transitions vs charge transfer
concepts.explanation: Colour in transition metal complexes arises from d-d transitions (incomplete d shell) or charge transfer (e.g., MnO₄⁻).
concepts.why_fragile: Students may confuse the two mechanisms.
concepts.common_error: Thinking all coloured compounds have d-d transitions.

concepts.name: Paramagnetism and unpaired electrons
concepts.explanation: Paramagnetism is due to unpaired electrons; spin-only formula μ = √(n(n+2)) BM.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may forget orbital contribution for heavy elements.

concepts.name: Chromate-dichromate equilibrium
concepts.explanation: 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O; yellow in alkaline, orange in acidic.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not remember the pH dependence.

concepts.name: KMnO₄ as oxidising agent: medium dependent products
concepts.explanation: In acid: Mn²⁺ (colourless); in neutral/weak alkaline: MnO₂ (brown); in strong alkaline: MnO₄²⁻ (green) then MnO₂.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not differentiate products.

concepts.name: Cu²⁺ + I⁻: redox and precipitation
concepts.explanation: Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂, itself reduced to Cu⁺ which precipitates as CuI (white). Excess I⁻ forms I₃⁻ (brown).
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not realise CuI is white and hidden.
concepts.common_error: Thinking the brown colour is CuI.

concepts.name: AgO structure: not Ag²⁺
concepts.explanation: AgO is actually Ag⁺[AgO₂]⁻ containing Ag(I) and Ag(III), diamagnetic.
concepts.why_fragile: Students expect AgO to be paramagnetic.

concepts.name: ZnO colour change on heating: F-centres
concepts.explanation: ZnO turns yellow on heating due to formation of F-centres (metal excess defects).
concepts.why_fragile: Students may think it's due to d-d transition.

concepts.name: Hydrogen's position in periodic table
concepts.explanation: Hydrogen resembles alkali metals (1 electron), halogens (one short of noble gas), and group 14 (half-filled shell).
concepts.why_fragile: Students expect hydrogen to be in one group only.

concepts.name: Free proton (H⁺) does not exist
concepts.explanation: Proton is extremely small, highly polarizing; always hydrated (H₃O⁺, H₃O₄⁺ etc.).
concepts.why_fragile: Writing H⁺ in equations.
concepts.common_error: Thinking H⁺ exists as free ion.

concepts.name: Hydrogen bonding – only with F, O, N (strong)
concepts.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are strongest with F, O, N; but also occur with Cl (weak) and C–H (weak) in special cases.
concepts.why_fragile: Thinking only F, O, N.

concepts.name: Intermolecular vs intramolecular H-bonding effect on properties
concepts.explanation: Intermolecular H-bonding raises melting/boiling points; intramolecular lowers them (for ortho isomers).
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing which effect occurs.
concepts.common_error: Expecting ortho isomers to have higher boiling points.

concepts.name: Isotope effect – differences in physical properties
concepts.explanation: H isotopes show large differences due to mass; D₂O has higher m.p., b.p., density; lower K_w.
concepts.why_fragile: Assuming isotopes have identical properties.

concepts.name: Ortho and para hydrogen – spin isomers, not chemical isomers
concepts.explanation: Difference in nuclear spin orientation; para has lower energy.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing with isotopes.

concepts.name: Metallic hydrides are nonstoichiometric
concepts.explanation: They are solid solutions; e.g., PdH₀.₇, TiH₁.₈₈.
concepts.why_fragile: Expecting fixed stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Covalent hydrides – boiling point trend exceptions
concepts.explanation: H₂O, NH₃, HF have anomalously high boiling points due to H-bonding; but HCl, HBr, HI do not.
concepts.why_fragile: Expecting smooth trend.

concepts.name: Acidity of ortho substituted phenols
concepts.explanation: Intramolecular H-bonding in o-nitrophenol reduces acidity; in o-hydroxy benzaldehyde also reduces.
concepts.why_fragile: Thinking ortho substitution always increases acidity.
concepts.common_error: Predicting o-nitrophenol more acidic than p-nitrophenol.

concepts.name: SN2 vs SN1 for hydrolysis of CCl₄ and NF₃
concepts.explanation: CCl₄ and NF₃ are inert to SN2 due to lack of vacant orbitals (C) or steric/repulsion (NF₃), but can undergo SN1 under drastic conditions.
concepts.why_fragile: Students assume all halides hydrolyse easily.

concepts.name: Partial hydrolysis of BF₃ and SiF₄ due to HF complexation
concepts.explanation: HF produced reacts with unhydrolysed starting material, forming complex acids, so only fraction hydrolysed.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may think hydrolysis is complete.
concepts.common_error: Expecting BF₃ + 3H₂O → B(OH)₃ + 3HF (which is not complete).

concepts.name: NCl₃ hydrolysis: attack on Cl, not N
concepts.explanation: N has no vacant orbital, so nucleophile attacks Cl, giving NH₃ and HCl (not HOCl).
concepts.why_fragile: Students assume attack on central atom.

concepts.name: Tautomerisation in PCl₃ hydrolysis vs AsCl₃
concepts.explanation: P(OH)₃ tautomerises to H₃PO₃ due to strong P=O bond; As(OH)₃ does not.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may think all Group 15 trichlorides give same type of acid.
concepts.common_error: Predicting H₃AsO₃ to have P–H bond.

concepts.name: Formation of oxychlorides for SbCl₃ and BiCl₃
concepts.explanation: Due to electropositive character, they form MOCl precipitates instead of M(OH)₃.
concepts.why_fragile: Students expect hydroxides.

concepts.name: Inertness of SF₆ due to steric crowding despite vacant d orbitals
concepts.explanation: Six F atoms shield S, preventing nucleophilic attack.
concepts.why_fragile: Students think availability of d orbitals ensures hydrolysis.

concepts.name: Redox hydrolysis of XeF₂ and XeF₄ vs SN2 for XeF₆
concepts.explanation: XeF₂ and XeF₄ undergo redox with water; XeF₆ undergoes simple substitution.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may apply same mechanism to all.

concepts.name: Basicity of acids from hydrolysis
concepts.explanation: H₃PO₃ is dibasic (two acidic H), H₃PO₂ monobasic; students may miscount.
concepts.why_fragile: Not all H atoms are acidic.

concepts.name: Mineral vs Ore
concepts.explanation: All ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores (only economically viable ones).
concepts.why_fragile: Students often use terms interchangeably.

concepts.name: Gangue and Flux
concepts.explanation: Gangue is the unwanted impurity in the ore; flux is added to remove gangue by forming slag.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing gangue with flux.

concepts.name: Calcination vs Roasting
concepts.explanation: Calcination is in limited air (for carbonates, hydroxides); roasting is in excess air (for sulphides).
concepts.why_fragile: Students mix up conditions and applications.

concepts.name: Self-reduction: no external reducing agent
concepts.explanation: Sulphide ore partially oxidised to oxide, which then reacts with remaining sulphide.
concepts.why_fragile: Students think external reducing agent is always needed.

concepts.name: Thermite reaction: Al as reducing agent
concepts.explanation: Al has high affinity for O₂; reaction is highly exothermic.
concepts.why_fragile: Why not use carbon for Cr, Mn?
concepts.common_error: Assuming carbon can reduce all oxides.

concepts.name: Electrolytic reduction: aqueous vs molten
concepts.explanation: Active metals (Na, Mg, Al) are extracted from molten salts, not aqueous, because water would be reduced instead.
concepts.why_fragile: Students think aqueous solutions can be used for all.
concepts.common_error: Using aqueous NaCl for sodium extraction.

concepts.name: Ellingham diagram: carbon line slope
concepts.explanation: C → CO line slopes downward, so at high T carbon can reduce many oxides.
concepts.why_fragile: Not understanding that CO₂ formation is less favoured at high T.
concepts.common_error: Thinking carbon reduction is always via C directly.

concepts.name: Zone refining: impurity prefers liquid phase
concepts.explanation: Impurities stay in molten zone; pure solid forms on cooling.
concepts.why_fragile: Students think impurities are removed as vapour.

concepts.name: Inert pair effect in Group 13/14/15
concepts.explanation: Inert pair effect: ns² electrons do not participate in bonding for heavier elements, leading to lower oxidation states (Tl⁺, Pb²⁺, Bi³⁺).
concepts.why_fragile: Students expect all elements to show highest group valency.
concepts.common_error: Assuming Tl(III) is more stable than Tl(I) (it's the reverse).

concepts.name: Borax bead test: colour indicates metal, not oxidation state
concepts.explanation: The bead colour comes from the metaborate of the metal; the original oxidation state cannot be inferred.
concepts.why_fragile: Students think the colour corresponds to the ion in the salt.
concepts.common_error: Trying to determine oxidation state from bead colour.

concepts.name: CO toxicity: haemoglobin complex
concepts.explanation: CO forms a complex with haemoglobin 300 times more stable than oxyhaemoglobin, preventing oxygen transport.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not understand the mechanism.
concepts.common_error: Thinking CO is toxic because it is acidic.

concepts.name: NO as a 3-electron donor in complexes
concepts.explanation: NO can donate a lone pair plus one electron from its π* orbital, making it a 3-electron donor.
concepts.why_fragile: Students treat NO as a 2-electron donor like CO.
concepts.common_error: Using 2-electron donation for EAN calculations with NO.

concepts.name: PCl₅ structure: covalent in gas, ionic in solid
concepts.explanation: In gas: trigonal bipyramidal (covalent); in solid: [PCl₄]⁺[PCl₆]⁻ (ionic).
concepts.why_fragile: Students assume one structure for all phases.
concepts.common_error: Drawing PCl₅ as ionic in gas phase.

concepts.name: NH₃ vs PH₃ basicity
concepts.explanation: NH₃ is much more basic because the lone pair is in an sp³ orbital; PH₃ lone pair is in an s orbital (less available).
concepts.why_fragile: Students expect similar basicity.
concepts.common_error: Thinking PH₃ is as basic as NH₃.

concepts.name: H₂O₂: oxidising and reducing agent
concepts.explanation: H₂O₂ can act as both oxidising agent (O⁻¹ → O⁻²) and reducing agent (O⁻¹ → O⁰).
concepts.why_fragile: Students often think it is only oxidising.
concepts.common_error: Writing H₂O₂ only as oxidising agent.

concepts.name: Ozone: polar and bent, not linear
concepts.explanation: O₃ is bent (116.8°), polar, and has resonance.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may think O₃ is linear like CO₂.

concepts.name: Xenon compounds: XeF₂ linear, XeF₄ square planar, XeF₆ distorted octahedral
concepts.explanation: VSEPR explains structures: XeF₂ (5 pairs, 3 LP), XeF₄ (6 pairs, 2 LP), XeF₆ (7 pairs, 1 LP).
concepts.why_fragile: Students may confuse with IF₇ or other interhalogens.

concepts.name: Period/Group prediction from configuration
concepts.explanation: Period = highest n; group for d‑block = (n−1)d + ns electrons; for p‑block = valence + 10; for f‑block = 3.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often forget to include ns electrons for d‑block, or use wrong formula for p‑block.
concepts.common_error: For Fe (Z=26): group = 6 (only d) instead of 8 (6+2).

concepts.name: Atomic radius types – covalent, metallic, van der Waals
concepts.explanation: Different radii measured under different conditions; order: vdW > metallic > covalent.
concepts.why_fragile: Students assume one radius for all; inert gases only have vdW.

concepts.name: Ionic radius – isoelectronic series
concepts.explanation: For same electrons, higher Z → smaller radius.
concepts.why_fragile: Students think higher charge means larger ion (wrong).

concepts.name: Ionization energy – anomalies (Be>B, N>O)
concepts.explanation: Due to stable configurations (ns², np³).
concepts.why_fragile: Expect monotonic increase; forget stability.
concepts.common_error: Assuming O has higher IE than N.

concepts.name: Electron affinity – Cl > F, N positive
concepts.explanation: F has small size causing repulsion; N has half‑filled p³.
concepts.why_fragile: Expect F to have highest EA.

concepts.name: Electronegativity – scales and formulas
concepts.explanation: Pauling (bond energy), Mulliken (IE+EA), Allred‑Rochow (Zeff/r²).
concepts.why_fragile: Confusion between scales and units.
concepts.common_error: Using Mulliken formula with kJ/mol (should be eV).

concepts.name: Hydration energy vs ionic mobility
concepts.explanation: Smaller ion has higher hydration, larger hydrated radius, lower mobility.
concepts.why_fragile: Think smaller ion moves faster.
concepts.common_error: Ordering Li⁺ > Na⁺ > K⁺ for mobility.

concepts.name: Mineral vs Ore (not directly in this chapter but relevant)
concepts.explanation: All ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores.
concepts.why_fragile: Students use terms interchangeably.

concepts.name: Gangue and Flux
concepts.explanation: Gangue is unwanted impurity in ore; flux is added to remove gangue.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing gangue with flux.

concepts.name: Carbonate vs Bicarbonate with phenolphthalein
concepts.explanation: CO₃²⁻ gives pink (hydrolysis produces enough OH⁻); HCO₃⁻ gives no colour.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not understand hydrolysis difference.

concepts.name: Sulphide test with sodium nitroprusside
concepts.explanation: Only S²⁻ (not H₂S) gives purple; H₂S requires alkali to generate S²⁻.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may pass H₂S directly into nitroprusside and expect colour.
concepts.common_error: Passing H₂S into sodium nitroprusside without alkali.

concepts.name: Brown ring test for NO₂⁻ vs NO₃⁻
concepts.explanation: Both give brown ring, but NO₂⁻ gives it with dilute acid; NO₃⁻ requires concentrated acid.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing the conditions.
concepts.common_error: Using conc. H₂SO₄ for NO₂⁻ (gives NO₂ fumes).

concepts.name: Chromyl chloride test interference
concepts.explanation: Br⁻ and I⁻ interfere (give Br₂/I₂ vapours); NO₂⁻, NO₃⁻, ClO₂⁻ also interfere.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not consider interferences.
concepts.common_error: Performing chromyl chloride test in presence of Br⁻.

concepts.name: Group separation – function of NH₄Cl
concepts.explanation: In Group III, NH₄Cl lowers OH⁻ so only Group III hydroxides (low Ksp) precipitate.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may not understand common ion effect.
concepts.common_error: Skipping NH₄Cl and getting Mg(OH)₂ precipitate.

concepts.name: Group II vs Group IV sulphide precipitation
concepts.explanation: Group II sulphides have very low Ksp, precipitate in acidic medium (low S²⁻); Group IV need higher S²⁻ (alkaline).
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing the pH conditions.
concepts.common_error: Using alkaline H₂S for Group II.

concepts.name: Fe²⁺ vs Fe³⁺ in group analysis
concepts.explanation: Fe²⁺ does not precipitate in Group III; it must be oxidised to Fe³⁺ by boiling with HNO₃.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may think Fe²⁺ gives Fe(OH)₂ in Group III (it doesn't; Fe(OH)₂ is Group IV).
concepts.common_error: Not oxidising Fe²⁺ before Group III.

concepts.name: Prussian blue vs Turnbull's blue
concepts.explanation: They are identical (Mössbauer spectroscopy).
concepts.why_fragile: Traditionally considered different.

concepts.name: Hydration and ionic mobility of alkali metals
concepts.explanation: Smaller ions (Li⁺) are heavily hydrated, so hydrated radius is large, leading to lower mobility; Cs⁺ has smallest hydrated radius, highest mobility.
concepts.why_fragile: Students expect smaller ions to move faster.
concepts.common_error: Thinking Li⁺ has higher ionic mobility than Cs⁺.

concepts.name: Reactivity of Li with water vs K
concepts.explanation: Li has most negative E° (-3.05V) but reacts gently; K reacts violently due to low melting point and kinetics.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing thermodynamics with kinetics.

concepts.name: Oxides of alkali metals: Li₂O, Na₂O₂, KO₂
concepts.explanation: Products depend on metal size; Li forms normal oxide, Na peroxide, K/Rb/Cs superoxide.
concepts.why_fragile: Students may think all form same oxide.

concepts.name: Diagonal relationship Li-Mg and Be-Al
concepts.explanation: Similarities arise from similar charge density; important for understanding anomalies.
concepts.why_fragile: Not obvious from periodic table position.

concepts.name: Hardness of water: temporary vs permanent
concepts.explanation: Temporary due to bicarbonates (removed by boiling); permanent due to sulphates/chlorides (removed by ion-exchange or precipitation).
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing the two types.

concepts.name: Solubility of Group 2 sulphates decreases down group
concepts.explanation: Hydration energy decreases faster than lattice energy; BaSO₄ is very insoluble.
concepts.why_fragile: Opposite trend to Group 1.

concepts.name: Difference between orbital and electron
concepts.explanation: Orbital is defined by n,l,m; electron is defined by n,l,m,s. An orbital can hold max 2 electrons.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often treat electrons and orbitals synonymously.
concepts.common_error: Saying 's orbital has spin' – spin is property of electron.

concepts.name: Quantum numbers – allowed ranges and interrelation
concepts.explanation: l ranges 0 to n−1; m ranges −l to +l; s is ±½. Not every combination is valid.
concepts.why_fragile: Confusing the meaning of each quantum number; forgetting that l depends on n.

concepts.name: Aufbau principle and (n+l) rule – exceptions
concepts.explanation: Electrons fill lowest energy orbitals, but exceptions (Cr, Cu, etc.) occur due to extra stability of half/full shells.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often assume strict Aufbau for all elements.

concepts.name: Hund's rule – maximum multiplicity and spin pairing
concepts.explanation: Degenerate orbitals are singly occupied with parallel spins before pairing.
concepts.why_fragile: Students pair electrons prematurely, especially for p³, d⁵.
concepts.common_error: Writing N as 1s²2s²2p⁶ (paired p) instead of 2p³ unpaired.

concepts.name: Slater's rule – grouping and contributions
concepts.explanation: Group as (1s)(2s,2p)(3s,3p)(3d)(4s,4p)...; contributions depend on shell and electron type.
concepts.why_fragile: Complex calculation; students forget to exclude electrons to the right.
concepts.common_error: Including 4s electrons when calculating σ for 3d (they contribute 0).

concepts.name: Nodal planes – orientation for d‑orbitals
concepts.explanation: Each d orbital has two nodal planes; for dz² there are conical nodes, not planes.
concepts.why_fragile: Students often think dz² has planar nodes.
concepts.common_error: Stating dz² has xz and yz planes (it has none).

concepts.name: Isoelectronic species – total electrons vs valence electrons
concepts.explanation: Traditional: same total electrons. Extended: same valence electrons.
concepts.why_fragile: JEE often uses both definitions; confusion arises.
concepts.common_error: Only considering total electrons for all cases.

concepts.name: Ionization order for d‑block cations
concepts.explanation: Remove ns electrons before (n−1)d, contrary to filling order.
concepts.why_fragile: Students assume the reverse (remove d first).

number_of_exceptions.description: All exceptions and traps from Chapter 3.

exceptions.standard_case: Octet rule applies to all molecules.
exceptions.exception: BeCl₂ (4 electrons), BF₃ (6), PF₅ (10), SF₆ (12), NO (odd).
exceptions.why_exception: Electron deficiency or availability of d orbitals.

exceptions.standard_case: VSEPR: lone pairs occupy equatorial positions in TBP.
exceptions.exception: For SN=7, lone pairs axial; for SN=6 with 2 LP, square planar.
exceptions.why_exception: Lone pairs prefer positions with more space.

exceptions.standard_case: Electronegativity decreases down a group.
exceptions.exception: Bond angle of PF₃ > PH₃ due to back bonding.

exceptions.standard_case: Ionic compounds are soluble in water.
exceptions.exception: AgCl, PbI₂, BaSO₄ are insoluble.

exceptions.standard_case: Melting point increases with lattice energy.
exceptions.exception: LiCl has lower m.p. than NaCl due to covalent character.

exceptions.standard_case: d orbitals participate in hybridization for hypervalent molecules.
exceptions.exception: In some cases (SF₆), d orbital involvement is debated.
exceptions.trap: Assuming d orbitals are always used.
exceptions.why_exception: d orbitals are high in energy; electronegative ligands contract them.

exceptions.standard_case: Acid strength increases with oxidation state.
exceptions.exception: H₃PO₂ > H₃PO₃ > H₃PO₄ (exception to OS rule).

exceptions.standard_case: All bond angles in TBP are either 90 or 120.
exceptions.exception: With different substituents, angles deviate (e.g., PF₃Cl₂).

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrogen bonding only occurs with F, O, N.
exceptions.exception: Weak C–H…O, etc., but strong only with F,O,N.

exceptions.standard_case: Inert gases are monatomic and non-polar.
exceptions.exception: Xe forms compounds with F and O (XeF₂, XeF₄, etc.).
exceptions.trap: Assuming noble gases are completely inert.

exceptions.standard_case: All d-block elements are metals.
exceptions.exception: Some d-block elements (like Zn, Cd, Hg) are not transition metals due to full d orbitals.
exceptions.why_exception: Definition requires partially filled d orbitals.

exceptions.standard_case: Ionic character increases with electronegativity difference.
exceptions.exception: In some cases, back bonding or covalent character can reduce ionic character (e.g., AgCl).
exceptions.trap: Assuming all NaCl-like compounds are purely ionic.

exceptions.standard_case: Polar molecules have higher boiling points than non-polar of similar size.
exceptions.exception: Sometimes molecular weight dominates (e.g., CCl₄ vs CHCl₃).

exceptions.standard_case: Sigma bonds are stronger than pi bonds.
exceptions.exception: In some cases, pi bonds can be strong (e.g., N₂).
exceptions.trap: Assuming pi bonds are always weaker.
exceptions.why_exception: Multiple bonds can have high bond order.

exceptions.standard_case: Molecules with zero dipole moment are non-polar.
exceptions.exception: Some molecules with zero dipole moment can still have polar bonds (e.g., CO₂).
exceptions.trap: Assuming CO₂ is non-polar (it is, but bonds are polar).

exceptions.standard_case: Resonance structures have equal energy.
exceptions.exception: Not all resonance structures contribute equally (e.g., some have charge separation).
exceptions.trap: Assuming all resonance structures are equal.

exceptions.standard_case: Coordination number in ionic compounds depends only on radius ratio.
exceptions.exception: Other factors like covalent character and packing can change CN.
exceptions.trap: Assuming radius ratio always predicts CN.

exceptions.standard_case: All oxides of metals are basic.
exceptions.exception: Transition metal oxides can be acidic (e.g., Mn₂O₇, CrO₃).
exceptions.why_exception: High oxidation states make oxides acidic.

exceptions.standard_case: All non-metal oxides are acidic.
exceptions.exception: Some non-metal oxides are neutral (e.g., CO, NO).
exceptions.trap: Assuming all non-metal oxides are acidic.
exceptions.why_exception: Low oxidation state oxides are neutral.

exceptions.standard_case: Bond length decreases with bond order.
exceptions.exception: Sometimes bond length may not follow due to lone pair repulsion (e.g., F₂).

exceptions.standard_case: Hybridization of central atom determines geometry.
exceptions.exception: Geometry also depends on lone pairs (VSEPR).

exceptions.standard_case: All compounds with coordinate bonds are ionic.
exceptions.exception: Coordinate bonds are covalent (e.g., NH₄⁺).

exceptions.standard_case: Metallic bonding is non-directional.
exceptions.exception: In some metals (e.g., Hg), there is some directionality.
exceptions.trap: Assuming all metals have free electron gas.

exceptions.standard_case: All ionic compounds are hard and brittle.
exceptions.exception: Some ionic compounds are soft (e.g., AgCl) due to covalent character.

exceptions.standard_case: Lattice energy is always exothermic.
exceptions.exception: Lattice energy is negative (exothermic) for formation.

exceptions.standard_case: F-centres are only in alkali halides.
exceptions.exception: F-centres can occur in other ionic crystals (e.g., CaO).
exceptions.why_exception: Any ionic crystal with anion vacancies.

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrogen bonding occurs only in protic solvents.
exceptions.exception: Can occur in solid state and gas phase as well.

exceptions.standard_case: Bond angles in hydrides follow periodic trend.
exceptions.exception: Exceptions due to back bonding (PF₃ > PH₃).

exceptions.standard_case: All p-block elements obey octet rule.
exceptions.exception: Third period and below can expand octet.

exceptions.standard_case: Diatomic molecules of halogens are non-polar.
exceptions.exception: Halogen interhalogens are polar (e.g., ClF).
exceptions.trap: Assuming all diatomic halogens are non-polar.

exceptions.standard_case: All d-block elements are transition elements.
exceptions.exception: Zn, Cd, Hg (d¹⁰) are not transition elements (no partially filled d orbital).

exceptions.standard_case: Chromium has electronic configuration [Ar]3d⁴4s².
exceptions.exception: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ (half-filled d).

exceptions.standard_case: Cu has [Ar]3d⁹4s².
exceptions.exception: Cu is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (filled d).

exceptions.standard_case: FeO is stoichiometric FeO.
exceptions.exception: FeO is nonstoichiometric (Fe₀.₈₄O to Fe₀.₉₅O).

exceptions.standard_case: AgCl is white and soluble in NH₃.
exceptions.exception: AgBr is pale yellow, sparingly soluble; AgI is yellow, insoluble.
exceptions.trap: Thinking all silver halides dissolve in NH₃.

exceptions.standard_case: CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue.
exceptions.exception: Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white; colour due to water of crystallisation.

exceptions.standard_case: FeCl₂ is a primary standard.
exceptions.exception: FeCl₂ is not a primary standard (easily oxidised).

exceptions.standard_case: KMnO₄ is a primary standard.
exceptions.exception: KMnO₄ is not a primary standard (decomposes, contains MnO₂).
exceptions.why_exception: Difficult to obtain pure; decomposes in light.

exceptions.standard_case: CuI₂ exists.
exceptions.exception: CuI₂ does not exist; Cu²⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂, forming CuI.
exceptions.why_exception: Cu²⁺ is oxidising, I⁻ is reducing.

exceptions.standard_case: AgO is paramagnetic.
exceptions.exception: AgO is diamagnetic (Ag⁺[AgO₂]⁻).

exceptions.standard_case: ZnO is white.
exceptions.exception: ZnO turns yellow on heating (F-centres).

exceptions.standard_case: All hydrides of Group 14 are covalent and volatile.
exceptions.exception: SiH₄, GeH₄, SnH₄ are covalent but show decreasing stability; carbon forms extensive catenation.
exceptions.trap: Assuming all group 14 hydrides behave like CH₄.

exceptions.standard_case: All ionic hydrides react with water to give H₂.
exceptions.exception: BeH₂ and MgH₂ are not purely ionic; they react but less violently.
exceptions.trap: Thinking all metal hydrides are ionic.
exceptions.why_exception: Be and Mg have some covalent character.

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrogen bonding occurs only with F, O, N.
exceptions.exception: Chlorine can form weak hydrogen bonds (e.g., in chloral hydrate, o-chlorophenol). Also C–H···O, π-hydrogen.
exceptions.trap: Ignoring H-bonding with Cl or π systems.
exceptions.why_exception: Polar C–H bonds or electron-rich π systems.

exceptions.standard_case: Heavy water has similar properties to normal water.
exceptions.exception: D₂O has higher m.p. (3.82°C), b.p. (101.42°C), density, lower K_w, lower solubility of salts.

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe.
exceptions.exception: On Earth's crust, it's only 0.152% by weight.
exceptions.why_exception: Earth's gravity too weak to hold H₂.

exceptions.standard_case: Metallic hydrides are conductors and have metallic lustre.
exceptions.exception: They are brittle and less dense than parent metal.

exceptions.standard_case: Boiling points of hydrides increase down the group.
exceptions.exception: For Group 15: NH₃ has anomalously high b.p.; for Group 16: H₂O; for Group 17: HF.

exceptions.standard_case: Acidity of dicarboxylic acids: Ka1 > Ka2.
exceptions.exception: For maleic acid, Ka1 is higher than fumaric; but Ka2 of maleic is lower than fumaric due to intramolecular H-bonding in the conjugate base of maleic? Actually Ka1 maleic > fumaric; Ka2 fumaric > maleic.
exceptions.trap: Assuming cis always more acidic for both steps.

exceptions.standard_case: Ortho and para hydrogen have same chemical properties.
exceptions.exception: They have different physical properties (thermal conductivity, specific heat) and different adsorption rates on surfaces.

exceptions.standard_case: All p-block hydrides are covalent and molecular.
exceptions.exception: Some are polymeric (e.g., B₂H₆ has bridge bonds; AlH₃ is polymeric).

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrogen is a good reducing agent.
exceptions.exception: It is not very reactive under normal conditions due to high bond energy (kinetic stability).
exceptions.trap: Expecting rapid reactions at room temperature.

exceptions.standard_case: Water is liquid at room temperature due to H-bonding.
exceptions.exception: H₂O has highest b.p. among group 16 hydrides, but HF and NH₃ also have anomalies.

exceptions.standard_case: Isotopes of hydrogen: protium, deuterium, tritium have similar chemical properties.
exceptions.exception: Rates of reaction differ (isotope effect); equilibrium constants differ.

exceptions.standard_case: Hydride ion (H⁻) is stable in ionic hydrides.
exceptions.exception: H⁻ is unstable in water; reacts vigorously.
exceptions.trap: Thinking H⁻ is stable in aqueous solution.

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrolysis of PCl₃ gives H₃PO₃ (dibasic).
exceptions.exception: Hydrolysis of NCl₃ gives NH₃ and HCl (not HOCl).

exceptions.standard_case: Complete hydrolysis of SiCl₄.
exceptions.exception: SiF₄ and BF₃ undergo partial hydrolysis.

exceptions.standard_case: Group 15 trichlorides give M(OH)₃.
exceptions.exception: SbCl₃ and BiCl₃ give MOCl (oxychlorides).

exceptions.standard_case: SF₄ hydrolyses readily.
exceptions.exception: SF₆ is inert.

exceptions.standard_case: Xenon fluorides hydrolyse to give oxyacids.
exceptions.exception: XeF₂ and XeF₄ undergo redox hydrolysis, XeF₆ does not.

exceptions.standard_case: SiH₄ hydrolyses with H₂ evolution.
exceptions.exception: CH₄ does not hydrolyse.

exceptions.standard_case: Hydrolysis of interhalogens gives HOA + HX where A is less electronegative.
exceptions.exception: Sometimes side products may form, but general rule holds.
exceptions.trap: Mistaking which halogen gets the OH.

exceptions.standard_case: Carbon reduction is used for most oxide ores.
exceptions.exception: Al₂O₃, MgO, TiO₂ cannot be reduced by carbon at practical temperatures (form carbides or too high T).
exceptions.trap: Assuming carbon can reduce any oxide.

exceptions.standard_case: Sulphide ores are concentrated by froth flotation.
exceptions.exception: Some sulphide ores (e.g., galena) can be separated using depressants (NaCN); ZnS is depressed.
exceptions.exam_relevance: Froth flotation of PbS and ZnS.

exceptions.standard_case: Roasting always converts sulphide to oxide.
exceptions.exception: In controlled conditions, sulphide can be converted to sulphate (e.g., ZnSO₄ at <850°C).
exceptions.why_exception: Excess air and lower temperature favour sulphate.

exceptions.standard_case: Self-reduction works for Cu, Pb, Hg.
exceptions.exception: Hg is extracted by thermal decomposition of HgS? Actually HgS is roasted to HgO then decomposed? In text, HgO is thermally decomposed; HgS is roasted. Self-reduction not for Hg.
exceptions.why_exception: Hg is volatile; thermal decomposition is used.

exceptions.standard_case: Electrolytic refining: anode is impure, cathode is pure.
exceptions.exception: For Al electrorefining, anode is impure Al + Cu melt, cathode is pure Al layer.
exceptions.trap: Assuming standard Cu setup for all.
exceptions.why_exception: Al is reactive; requires different cell design.

exceptions.standard_case: Flux is always added to remove acidic gangue with basic flux (and vice versa).
exceptions.exception: Sometimes flux is not needed if gangue is self-fluxing (e.g., limestone contains CaO and SiO₂).
exceptions.why_exception: Some ores have gangue that can act as flux.

exceptions.standard_case: Anode mud contains only noble metals (Au, Ag, Pt).
exceptions.exception: In Cu electrorefining, some less noble metals (Ni, Fe, Zn) dissolve; anode mud has Au, Ag, Pt, and sometimes PbSO₄, etc.
exceptions.why_exception: Insoluble impurities like PbSO₄ may also be present.

exceptions.standard_case: Bessemer process for steel uses acid lining.
exceptions.exception: If pig iron contains P, basic lining (dolomite) is used (Thomas process).
exceptions.why_exception: Basic lining removes P as slag.

exceptions.standard_case: Roasting is necessary for sulphide ores.
exceptions.exception: For self-reduction, only partial roasting is needed.
exceptions.why_exception: Complete roasting would oxidise all sulphide; no self-reduction.

exceptions.standard_case: Carbon reduction gives molten metal.
exceptions.exception: For Zn, the metal is obtained as vapour (distilled) because Zn boils at 920°C, below smelting temperature.

exceptions.standard_case: Calcination of carbonate ores gives oxide and CO₂.
exceptions.exception: Some carbonates (e.g., MgCO₃) require higher temperature; but still gives oxide.

exceptions.standard_case: Poling is used for Cu and Sn.
exceptions.exception: Poling is also used for other metals? Not mentioned.

exceptions.standard_case: Vapour phase refining is only for Ni (Mond).
exceptions.exception: Van Arkel process for Zr, Ti, B also uses vapour phase.

exceptions.standard_case: Boron is a non-metal, forms covalent compounds.
exceptions.exception: Boron shows some metallic properties; forms borides.
exceptions.why_exception: Small size and high ionisation energy.

exceptions.standard_case: Group 13 elements show +3 oxidation state.
exceptions.exception: Tl shows stable +1 (inert pair effect); Ga and In also show +1.

exceptions.standard_case: CO₂ is an acidic oxide.
exceptions.exception: CO is a neutral oxide (not acidic).
exceptions.why_exception: CO is not an acid anhydride.

exceptions.standard_case: N₂O is a neutral oxide.
exceptions.exception: N₂O₃ is acidic (anhydride of HNO₂), N₂O₅ acidic.
exceptions.trap: Thinking all N oxides are acidic.

exceptions.standard_case: Phosphorus acid H₃PO₃ is tribasic.
exceptions.exception: H₃PO₃ is dibasic (only two acidic H).
exceptions.trap: Assuming all three H are acidic.

exceptions.standard_case: Hypophosphorous acid H₃PO₂ is tribasic.
exceptions.exception: H₃PO₂ is monobasic (only one acidic H).

exceptions.standard_case: All chlorides give chromyl chloride test.
exceptions.exception: AgCl, HgCl₂, Hg₂Cl₂, PbCl₄, SnCl₄ do not respond.
exceptions.why_exception: Covalent or insoluble, insufficient free Cl⁻.

exceptions.standard_case: Fluorine has highest electron affinity.
exceptions.exception: Chlorine has higher electron affinity than fluorine.
exceptions.why_exception: F is too small; electron repulsion.

exceptions.standard_case: HF is a strong acid.
exceptions.exception: HF is a weak acid (pKa 3.2) due to strong H–F bond and H-bonding.
exceptions.trap: Assuming HF is strong like HCl.
exceptions.why_exception: High bond energy and hydration effects.

exceptions.standard_case: All noble gases are inert.
exceptions.exception: Xe forms compounds (XeF₂, XeF₄, XeF₆, XeO₃, etc.); KrF₂ also known.

exceptions.standard_case: SiO₂ is isostructural with CO₂.
exceptions.exception: SiO₂ is not molecular like CO₂; it has a giant 3D network.
exceptions.trap: Assuming SiO₂ is linear like CO₂.
exceptions.why_exception: Si cannot form pπ-pπ bonds; uses σ bonds only.

exceptions.standard_case: All allotropes of carbon are conductors.
exceptions.exception: Diamond is an insulator; graphite is a conductor.

exceptions.standard_case: O₂ is diamagnetic.
exceptions.exception: O₂ is paramagnetic (two unpaired electrons).
exceptions.trap: Assuming O₂ is diamagnetic like N₂.
exceptions.why_exception: Molecular orbital theory: unpaired electrons in π* orbitals.

exceptions.standard_case: H₂S is a strong acid.
exceptions.exception: H₂S is a weak acid (dibasic).

exceptions.standard_case: SF₆ is reactive.
exceptions.exception: SF₆ is extremely inert.
exceptions.why_exception: Steric protection by six F atoms.

exceptions.standard_case: Atomic radius increases down a group.
exceptions.exception: Al ≈ Ga (3d¹⁰ poor shielding) and In ≈ Tl (4f¹⁴ poor shielding).
exceptions.why_exception: d/f electrons do not shield well, increasing Zeff.

exceptions.standard_case: Ionization energy decreases down a group.
exceptions.exception: Al ≈ Ga, In < Tl (Group 13).
exceptions.trap: Assuming Tl has lower IE than In.
exceptions.why_exception: Lanthanide contraction in Tl raises IE.

exceptions.standard_case: Electron affinity increases across a period.
exceptions.exception: N < C (half‑filled), also O < F? Actually F > O, but N is lower than C. Also P < Si, As < Ge, Sb < Sn, and Pb < Bi.
exceptions.trap: Assuming N has higher EA than C.

exceptions.standard_case: Electronegativity: inert gases have zero.
exceptions.exception: Xe can have small EN due to compounds with F/O.
exceptions.trap: Assigning positive EN to all noble gases.

exceptions.standard_case: Acid strength of oxoacids increases with oxidation state.
exceptions.exception: H₃PO₂ (monobasic) > H₃PO₃ (dibasic) > H₃PO₄ (tribasic) – exception.
exceptions.why_exception: Number of O‑H bonds and P‑H bonds.

exceptions.standard_case: Ionic radius: cation < atom < anion.
exceptions.exception: H⁻ is larger than F⁻ (H⁻: 208 pm, F⁻: 133 pm).

exceptions.standard_case: Lattice energy: higher charge → higher.
exceptions.exception: Some covalent character reduces lattice energy (e.g., AgCl).
exceptions.trap: Assuming purely ionic model always works.

exceptions.standard_case: All carbonates give CO₂ on heating.
exceptions.exception: Alkali metal carbonates (Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃, Rb₂CO₃, Cs₂CO₃) do not decompose on heating.

exceptions.standard_case: All nitrates give NO₂ on heating.
exceptions.exception: Alkali nitrates (NaNO₃, KNO₃) give nitrite + O₂, not NO₂.

exceptions.standard_case: AgCl is soluble in NH₃.
exceptions.exception: AgBr is sparingly soluble; AgI is insoluble.
exceptions.trap: Thinking all silver halides dissolve in NH₃.

exceptions.standard_case: Chlorides give chromyl chloride test.
exceptions.exception: AgCl, HgCl₂, Hg₂Cl₂, PbCl₄, SnCl₄ do not respond because they are covalent/insoluble.
exceptions.trap: Performing chromyl chloride test on AgCl.

exceptions.standard_case: Br⁻ gives red layer with chlorine water.
exceptions.exception: Excess chlorine water oxidises Br₂ to BrCl (pale yellow).
exceptions.trap: Using excess chlorine water and expecting red layer.

exceptions.standard_case: I⁻ gives violet layer with chlorine water.
exceptions.exception: Excess chlorine water oxidises I₂ to IO₃⁻ (colourless).

exceptions.standard_case: Sulphides of Group II are insoluble in yellow ammonium sulphide.
exceptions.exception: Group IIB sulphides (As₂S₃, Sb₂S₃, SnS, SnS₂) are soluble in YAS.
exceptions.trap: Assuming all Group II sulphides are insoluble.

exceptions.standard_case: CdS is yellow and soluble in YAS?
exceptions.exception: CdS is yellow but insoluble in YAS (unlike As₂S₃).
exceptions.why_exception: CdS does not form soluble thio complex.

exceptions.standard_case: MnS is buff coloured.
exceptions.exception: MnS is buff or flesh coloured, soluble in acetic acid.
exceptions.why_exception: MnS is Group IV; dissolves in dilute acids.

exceptions.standard_case: Fe³⁺ + S²⁻ gives Fe₂S₃ (black).
exceptions.exception: Fe³⁺ + S²⁻ actually gives FeS (black) + S (white) due to redox: 2Fe³⁺ + S²⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + S; then Fe²⁺ + S²⁻ → FeS.

exceptions.standard_case: Brown ring test for nitrate: use FeSO₄ + conc. H₂SO₄.
exceptions.exception: Ca(NO₃)₂, Ba(NO₃)₂, Pb(NO₃)₂ give sulphate precipitates and do not give ring.

exceptions.standard_case: Borax bead test is for coloured salts.
exceptions.exception: Some coloured salts may not give bead; some colourless salts may give bead.
exceptions.trap: Trying bead test for all salts.
exceptions.why_exception: Only transition metals give coloured beads.

exceptions.standard_case: All sodium salts are soluble.
exceptions.exception: NaHCO₃ is sparingly soluble (but still soluble enough).
exceptions.trap: Assuming NaHCO₃ is insoluble? Actually it is soluble.
exceptions.why_exception: Not an exception; just a note.

exceptions.standard_case: Ammonium salts give NH₃ with NaOH.
exceptions.exception: Some ammonium salts may give other gases if anion is oxidising (e.g., NH₄NO₃ gives N₂O).

exceptions.standard_case: Group V cations: Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺ all give white carbonates.
exceptions.exception: CaCO₃ is soluble in CO₂ (as bicarbonate); SrCO₃ and BaCO₃ are not.
exceptions.trap: Thinking all carbonates behave the same.

exceptions.standard_case: Pb²⁺ is in Group I.
exceptions.exception: Pb²⁺ also appears in Group II because PbCl₂ is sparingly soluble and some Pb²⁺ remains in solution.
exceptions.trap: Expecting Pb²⁺ only in Group I.

exceptions.standard_case: AgCl is white and soluble in NH₃.
exceptions.exception: AgCl also dissolves in Na₂S₂O₃ and KCN.

exceptions.standard_case: Iodide gives yellow precipitate with AgNO₃.
exceptions.exception: AgI is yellow and insoluble in NH₃, but soluble in Na₂S₂O₃ and KCN.
exceptions.trap: Thinking AgI is insoluble in all.
exceptions.why_exception: Complex formation with thiosulphate and cyanide.

exceptions.standard_case: Borate gives green flame with methanol.
exceptions.exception: Cu and Ba salts also give green flame; use CaF₂ + H₂SO₄ to produce BF₃ if Cu/Ba interfere.
exceptions.trap: Performing green flame test directly on unknown sample.

exceptions.standard_case: Phosphate gives canary yellow precipitate with ammonium molybdate.
exceptions.exception: Arsenate also gives similar precipitate, but only on boiling.

exceptions.standard_case: Alkali metals form normal oxides on burning.
exceptions.exception: Na forms peroxide (Na₂O₂), K/Rb/Cs form superoxides (MO₂).
exceptions.why_exception: Large cations stabilize larger anions (O₂²⁻, O₂⁻).

exceptions.standard_case: All alkali metals form nitrides.
exceptions.exception: Only Li forms stable nitride Li₃N.
exceptions.why_exception: Small Li⁺ gives high lattice energy.

exceptions.standard_case: Alkali metal bicarbonates exist as solids.
exceptions.exception: LiHCO₃ does not exist in solid form (only in solution).
exceptions.why_exception: Li⁺ is too small to stabilize HCO₃⁻ lattice.

exceptions.standard_case: Alkaline earth carbonates are stable.
exceptions.exception: BeCO₃ decomposes below 100°C; MgCO₃ decomposes at ~540°C.

exceptions.standard_case: Be is a metal like others in Group 2.
exceptions.exception: Be is amphoteric, forms covalent compounds, complexes, and polymeric halides.
exceptions.trap: Expecting Be to behave like Ca.
exceptions.why_exception: Very small size and high charge density.

exceptions.standard_case: All alkaline earth metals form peroxides.
exceptions.exception: BeO₂ is not known; MgO₂ can be made but not stable; CaO₂ can be made as hydrate; SrO₂ and BaO₂ are stable.
exceptions.why_exception: Small cations cannot stabilize peroxide ion.

exceptions.standard_case: CaC₂ gives acetylene on hydrolysis.
exceptions.exception: Be₂C gives methane; Mg₂C₃ gives propyne.
exceptions.trap: Expecting all carbides to give acetylene.
exceptions.why_exception: Different carbide ions: C₂²⁻, C⁴⁻, C₃⁴⁻.

exceptions.standard_case: Alkali metal halides are ionic and soluble.
exceptions.exception: LiF is sparingly soluble due to high lattice energy.
exceptions.why_exception: Small Li⁺ and F⁻ give high lattice energy.

exceptions.standard_case: Group 2 nitrates decompose to oxide + NO₂ + O₂.
exceptions.exception: Be(NO₃)₂ gives basic nitrate [Be₄O(NO₃)₆] at 125°C.

exceptions.standard_case: BaSO₄ is insoluble in water.
exceptions.exception: It is used as a barium meal because it is opaque to X-rays and non-toxic.

exceptions.exception: Cr: [Ar]3d⁵4s¹; Cu: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; Mo: [Kr]4d⁵5s¹; Nb: [Kr]4d⁴5s¹? Actually Nb is [Kr]4d⁴5s¹? Wait: from text: Nb: [Kr]4d⁴5s¹? The PDF lists: Nb: [Kr]4d⁴5s¹? exceptions.why_exception: Extra stability from half/full d subshells due to exchange energy and symmetry.

exceptions.standard_case: Slater's rule: electrons in same shell contribute 0.35.
exceptions.exception: For 1s electrons, the other 1s electron contributes 0.3 (not 0.35).
exceptions.why_exception: Special case for the innermost shell.

exceptions.standard_case: In d‑block cations, remove ns first.
exceptions.exception: For Cr and Cu, the removal still follows ns first, but the resulting configuration may have exceptions (e.g., Cu²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁹).
exceptions.why_exception: 4s is higher in energy for cations.

exceptions.standard_case: Spin multiplicity M = 2|S|+1.
exceptions.exception: For d⁵ (half‑filled), S=5/2, M=6; for d¹⁰ (full), S=0, M=1.

exceptions.standard_case: Nodal planes: d orbitals have two planes.
exceptions.exception: dz² has zero nodal planes (two conical nodal surfaces).

exceptions.standard_case: In a period, Zeff increases left to right.
exceptions.exception: Slater's rule may give slight anomalies, but trend holds.

exceptions.standard_case: Isoelectronic species have same number of electrons.
exceptions.exception: Extended definition includes same valence electrons (e.g., ClO₄⁻, BrO₄⁻).
